newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's January unemployment flat at 9.7 percent.
newsitem.headline: Canada's January unemployment flat at 9.7 percent.

text.p: Canada's unemployment rate remained unchanged at 9.7 percent in January from December as the economy created only 5,100 new jobs, Statistics Canada, a government agency, said on Friday.
Full-time employment rose by 32,400 from the month before, while part-time employment fell by 27,300.
A Reuters survey of economists had forecast the unemployment rate to drop to 9.6 percent.
Economists said a pause in employment gains was to be expected after the unemployment rate fell to 9.7 percent in December from 10.0 percent in November and the economy created 34,000 jobs.

"I think if you look at the headline numbers, it may seem a bit disappointing with only minor job gains of around 5,000. But if you scratch the surface and look a little deeper, you see that this report is not that tepid," said Canada Trust economist Steve Saldanha.
"In fact, you had a job gain full-time of 32,000. That's the kind of indicator that we look for going forward to be the underpinning of a consumer renaissance this year," he said.
Statistics Canada said total employment has risen by 91,000, or 0.7 percent, since September 1996. Of all the jobs created, 80,000 were full-time.
"The employment numbers are still giving indications of employment strengthening," said Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist at Bank of Montreal.

"I am a little bit disappointed that we are not seeing stronger gains but we have come off three months of employment growth and the January data suggest that we are managing to hold onto those gains."
Employment in the goods-producing sector was little changed in January and employment in the construction sector rose by 19,000.
The utilities industry lost 11,000 jobs in the month. Employment in manufacturing was little changed after declining by 42,000 in the previous three months.
There was also little change in service sector employment in January, leaving gains in the past year at only 38,000 jobs, Statistics Canada said.
Public employment was virtually unchanged in the month and a strong gain in self-employment was offset by a large decline in private sector employment.
